title: Monsoon Chilli Paneer: A Crispy Indo-Chinese Classic Ready in 35 Minutes
excerpt: This restaurant-style chilli paneer recipe delivers golden, crunchy paneer cubes tossed in a spicy, tangy sauce — perfect for rainy-evening cravings at home.
body:
• A complete restaurant-style chilli paneer recipe using a light cornflour-and-flour batter for maximum crispiness, with a tangy sauce built from soy, chilli sauce, ketchup, and vinegar.
  • The key to crispy paneer: pat cubes dry before battering, fry in batches over medium heat to avoid overcrowding, and add them to the sauce only at the very end so they stay crunchy.
  • This Indo-Chinese staple works as a starter, a side with fried rice or hakka noodles, or a standalone monsoon snack — ready from prep to plate in about 35 minutes.

Why Chilli Paneer Hits Different in the Monsoon

There is something about rain on the windows that makes Indo-Chinese food feel necessary. Chilli paneer — that gloriously inauthentic collision of Indian spice instincts and Chinese stir-fry technique — is the monsoon's signature comfort food. Crispy on the outside, soft inside, coated in a sauce that manages to be spicy, sweet, sour, and savory at once.

The dish emerged from Kolkata's Chinese-Indian kitchens decades ago and has since become one of the most ordered starters at Indian restaurants worldwide. Making it at home takes about 35 minutes and delivers results that rival your local Indo-Chinese spot.

"Fry the paneer in batches — do not crowd the pan — turning occasionally until golden and crisp on all sides, about 5–7 minutes."

Ingredients

For the paneer batter:

  • 250g paneer, cut into ¾-inch cubes
  • 3 tablespoons cornflour (cornstarch)
  • 2 tablespoons all-purpose flour (maida)
  • ¼ teaspoon Kashmiri red chilli powder
  • ¼ teaspoon black pepper
  • ½ teaspoon salt
  • 5–6 tablespoons water (enough for a smooth, medium-thick batter)
  • Oil for shallow frying

For the stir-fry:

  • 1 tablespoon oil (sesame oil adds depth)
  • 3 cloves garlic, finely minced
  • 1-inch piece of ginger, finely minced
  • 2 green chillies, slit lengthwise
  • 1 medium onion, cut into chunky squares
  • 1 bell pepper (capsicum), cut into similar-sized squares
  • 4 spring onions — whites chopped for cooking, greens reserved for garnish

For the sauce:

  • 2 tablespoons soy sauce
  • 2 tablespoons tomato ketchup
  • 1 tablespoon chilli sauce (adjust to taste)
  • 1 teaspoon rice vinegar or white vinegar
  • ½ teaspoon sugar (optional, balances acidity)
  • 1 teaspoon cornflour mixed into 3 tablespoons water (the slurry that thickens everything)

Method

Step 1: Batter and fry the paneer. Pat the paneer cubes dry — moisture is the enemy of crispiness. Whisk the cornflour, flour, chilli powder, pepper, salt, and water into a smooth batter. Toss the paneer cubes in, coating each piece evenly. Heat oil in a pan over medium heat. Fry the paneer in batches — do not crowd the pan — turning occasionally until golden and crisp on all sides, about 5–7 minutes. Drain on paper towels.

Step 2: Build the aromatics. In a wok or large frying pan, heat a tablespoon of oil over high heat. Add the garlic, ginger, and green chillies. Stir-fry for 30 seconds until fragrant — you want sizzle, not burning.

Step 3: Add the vegetables. Toss in the onion squares, bell pepper, and spring onion whites. Stir-fry on high heat for 1–2 minutes. You want them crisp-tender, still with some bite. Soggy vegetables kill this dish.

Step 4: Sauce it. Add the soy sauce, ketchup, chilli sauce, vinegar, and sugar. Stir everything together and let it bubble for 30 seconds. Pour in the cornflour slurry and stir continuously until the sauce thickens and turns glossy — about a minute.

Step 5: Toss in the paneer. Add the fried paneer cubes and toss gently to coat every piece. Do this quickly — the paneer should spend just 30 seconds in the sauce, enough to coat but not enough to lose its crunch.

Step 6: Garnish and serve. Top with the reserved spring onion greens. Serve immediately as a starter, or alongside egg fried rice or hakka noodles for a full meal.

Tips From the Indo-Chinese Kitchen

The difference between good and great chilli paneer comes down to three things. First, the paneer itself — fresh block paneer holds its shape better than pre-packaged varieties. Soaking cubes in hot water for 20 minutes before battering softens them if they feel dry. Second, the oil temperature matters. Too hot and the batter burns before the paneer warms through. Too cool and the cubes absorb oil and go limp. Medium heat is the sweet spot. Third, timing the sauce toss. Every second the paneer sits in liquid, it loses crispiness. Get the sauce ready, add the paneer, toss, plate, eat.

For an air-fryer version, toss coated cubes with a tablespoon of oil and air-fry at 200°C for 4–5 minutes, flipping halfway. The results are lighter, with a slightly different crunch — less shatteringly crisp than deep-fried, but honestly delicious.
